subject: Medicine
summary: Opportunistic infections occur when the immune system is weakened, allowing normally harmless organisms to cause disease. Clinicians must identify the underlying immune defect, recognize atypical presentations, and use targeted therapy while managing complications.

sections.p: Opportunistic infections (OIs) are infections that exploit a compromised host defense, often seen in HIV, transplant, or malignancy patients. Diagnosis combines clinical suspicion, imaging, and microbiology, guided by the patient’s immune status.
b: Identify immune defect (e.g., CD4 count, neutropenia)
Look for atypical pathogens (Pneumocystis, CMV, Toxoplasma)

t.b: Is the patient at risk for specific OIs? A count <200 cells/µL indicates high risk for Pneumocystis and cryptococcal meningitis.
Detects infiltrates suggestive of Pneumocystis or fungal pneumonia; a diffuse ground‑glass pattern raises suspicion.
Positive PCR in blood or CSF confirms CMV disease; a high viral load correlates with severity.
Positive result in serum or CSF indicates cryptococcal meningitis; a high titer predicts worse outcome.
Positive test suggests latent TB; in an immunocompromised host it may progress to active disease.

sections.p: Severity is graded by organ involvement and immune status. For example, Pneumocystis pneumonia is staged by PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio; CMV retinitis severity is staged by retinal lesion size.
b: Use WHO HIV staging for overall risk

t.b: A ratio <200 mmHg indicates severe hypoxia requiring high‑flow oxygen or ventilation.
Lesions >5 mm require urgent antiviral therapy.

sections.p: The most common causes of OIs are HIV infection, chemotherapy‑induced neutropenia, organ transplantation, and congenital immunodeficiencies. In low‑resource settings, TB, malaria, and bacterial sepsis often coexist and mask OIs.
b: HIV (low CD4)
Chemotherapy (neutropenia)
Transplant (immunosuppression)
Congenital immunodeficiency (e.g., SCID)

t.b: High load correlates with rapid CD4 decline and higher OI risk.
ANC <500 cells/µL predicts bacterial and fungal infections.

sections.p: Presentation is often subtle and overlaps with common infections. Fever, weight loss, and night sweats are common, but organ‑specific signs (e.g., cough, visual changes, seizures) guide diagnosis.
b: Fever + weight loss
Cough + dyspnea
Visual changes + eye pain

t.b: Crackles or wheeze may indicate Pneumocystis or fungal pneumonia.
Cherry red spots or retinal hemorrhages suggest CMV retinitis.

sections.p: Investigation strategy prioritises rapid, affordable tests. When resources are limited, clinical algorithms and empirical therapy are essential.
b: Rapid antigen tests

t.b: Detects Plasmodium falciparum; a positive result rules out malaria as sole cause of fever.
Identifies acid‑fast bacilli in sputum; a positive result confirms TB.
Silver stain of induced sputum shows cysts; a positive result confirms PCP.
Detects HSV DNA in CSF; a positive result confirms HSV encephalitis.

sections.p: Red flags include rapid deterioration, severe hypoxia, seizures, or shock. Complications can be organ failure, secondary infections, or drug toxicity.
b: Sudden drop in oxygen saturation

t.b: Hypotension indicates septic shock; requires fluid resuscitation and vasopressors.
Hypoglycaemia in a septic patient signals metabolic crisis.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypoxia, sudden neurological decline, shock, or any sign of organ failure

faq.q: What is the most common opportunistic infection in HIV patients?
faq.a: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, especially when CD4 counts fall below 200 cells/µL.

faq.q: How do I differentiate bacterial sepsis from an opportunistic infection in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: Look for atypical pathogens (e.g., Pneumocystis, CMV) and consider the patient’s immune status; empirical broad‑spectrum antibiotics plus targeted therapy may be needed.

faq.q: Can a patient with a low CD4 count develop malaria?
faq.a: Yes; malaria can coexist and complicate the clinical picture, so malaria testing should be done even in immunocompromised patients.

exam: Explain why Pneumocystis pneumonia is more common in patients with CD4 counts <200 cells/µL.
Describe the diagnostic approach to a patient with suspected CMV retinitis in a resource‑limited setting.
Outline the first‑line management of cryptococcal meningitis and the rationale for each drug choice.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam reveal the immune defect, exposure risk and organ involvement that distinguish opportunistic infections from common bacterial diseases.
b: Immune status: HIV diagnosis, latest CD4 count, ART adherence, recent chemotherapy cycles, neutrophil trends, transplant date and immunosuppressants.
Recent exposures: travel, animal contact, soil, bird droppings, contaminated water, sexual partners, blood products.
Symptoms by organ: cough, dyspnoea, chest pain, visual changes, headache, focal neurologic deficits, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, oral lesions, skin rashes.
Systemic clues: fever pattern, weight loss, night sweats, chronic fatigue, recent opportunistic prophylaxis failures.
Medication history: TMP‑SMX use, sulfa allergy, renal/hepatic impairment, concomitant steroids, herbal remedies.

t.b: Look for cachexia, oral thrush, skin lesions, lymphadenopathy; positive findings suggest chronic immunosuppression but cannot identify the pathogen.

Percussion for dullness, auscultation for fine crackles (PCP) versus bronchial breath sounds (TB); a positive fine crackle suggests interstitial process but cannot differentiate PCP from viral pneumonitis.
Direct ophthalmoscopy for CMV retinitis (hemorrhagic brush‑stroke lesions); a positive view confirms ocular CMV but cannot rule out other retinal infections without PCR.
Assess mental status, cranial nerves, motor strength, reflexes, and meningeal signs; focal deficits point to CNS OI (cryptococcal meningitis, toxoplasmosis) but do not specify organism.
Palpate for hepatosplenomegaly (histoplasmosis, disseminated TB); percussion for shifting dullness (ascites) suggests advanced disease but does not identify cause.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Prioritise rapid, affordable tests; when unavailable, use clinical algorithms and surrogate markers.
b: CBC with differential – neutrophils <1000/µL raise risk of invasive fungal disease; lymphopenia with CD4 <200/µL predicts PCP, CMV, MAC.
Serum CD4 count – <200/µL indicates PCP prophylaxis; <50/µL predicts CMV disease, MAC, disseminated histoplasmosis.
Chest X‑ray – diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates suggest PCP; cavitary lesions favour TB; miliary pattern may be disseminated fungal infection.
Sputum Gram stain and AFB – positive AFB confirms TB; negative AFB does not exclude PCP.
Serum (1→3)-β‑D‑glucan – elevated (>80 pg/mL) supports PCP, candidiasis, aspergillosis; normal does not rule out TB or viral infections.
Cryptococcal antigen (serum or CSF) – positive latex agglutination confirms cryptococcal meningitis; titers guide severity.
CMV PCR (blood) – quantitative load >1000 copies/mL in symptomatic patient supports CMV disease; unavailable tests → rely on fundoscopic findings.
India ink stain of CSF – visualises encapsulated yeast; positive confirms cryptococcus, but sensitivity low; if unavailable, treat on antigen positivity.

t.a: Serum albumin and ascitic fluid albumin
t.b: Calculate SAAG = serum albumin – ascitic albumin; SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension (e.g., TB peritonitis), SAAG <1.1 g/dL suggests exudative OI (peritoneal cryptococcosis).
A falling CD4 <50/µL triggers prophylaxis for MAC and CMV; stable >200/µL may allow stopping PCP prophylaxis.
Opening pressure >250 mm H₂O suggests cryptococcal meningitis; therapeutic taps reduce pressure; unavailable → monitor for papilledema clinically.
Weekly CBC; neutrophils <0.5×10⁹/L or creatinine rise >25% mandates dose reduction or switch; if labs unavailable, watch for cytopenia clinically.
Check transaminases; stop if >5× ULN or platelets <25×10⁹/L; if labs not available, limit duration to 2 weeks and monitor for hepatic signs.

sections.p: Use pathogen‑specific criteria combined with immune status to stage disease and guide therapy intensity.
b: PCP: Diagnosis – induced sputum or BAL showing cysts on methenamine silver; severity – PaO₂ <70 mmHg or A‑a gradient >35 mmHg, or respiratory rate >30/min.
Cryptococcal meningitis: Diagnosis – positive CSF cryptococcal antigen or culture; staging – opening pressure >250 mm H₂O or CSF fungal burden >10⁴ CFU/mL indicates severe disease.
CMV retinitis: Diagnosis – characteristic fundoscopic lesions; severity – lesions involving >1 quadrant or bilateral disease require systemic therapy.
Disseminated MAC: Diagnosis – blood culture positive for Mycobacterium avium complex; staging – CD4 <50/µL and systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss) denote advanced infection.
Histoplasmosis (disseminated): Diagnosis – urine antigen positive; severity – hepatic involvement, cytopenias, or CD4 <150/µL indicate need for induction therapy.

sections.p: Several common infections mimic OIs; careful history, targeted tests and organ‑specific signs separate them.

t.b: TB: cavitary lesions, positive sputum AFB, night sweats; PCP: diffuse bilateral ground‑glass infiltrates, normal sputum, CD4 <200/µL. GeneXpert or sputum AFB distinguishes TB.
Bacterial: neutrophilic CSF, low glucose, high protein, opening pressure high; cryptococcal: lymphocytic CSF, India ink positive, cryptococcal antigen positive, opening pressure >250 mm H₂O.

t.a: Toxoplasma encephalitis vs primary CNS lymphoma (HIV)
t.b: Toxoplasma: multiple ring‑enhancing lesions, CD4 <100/µL, positive Toxoplasma IgG; lymphoma: solitary lesion, mass effect, EBV DNA in CSF. Empiric anti‑toxoplasma therapy and repeat imaging differentiate.
Candida: white plaques, endoscopy shows pseudomembranes, culture grows yeast; CMV: linear ulcerations, CMV PCR positive. Endoscopy required for definitive distinction.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides clinicians from immediate stabilization to definitive therapy, monitoring, and criteria for escalation or referral in opportunistic infections.
b: 1. Stabilise airway, breathing, circulation; give supplemental O2 if PaO2 < 60 mmHg, consider non‑invasive support first.
2. Identify the likely pathogen using CD4 or neutrophil count and organ involvement; start empiric therapy covering the most probable OI.

3. Initiate definitive antimicrobial regimen: e.g., TMP‑SMX for PCP, ganciclovir for CMV, amphotericin B + flucytosine for cryptococcal meningitis, fluconazole for candidiasis, appropriate anti‑TB drugs if TB co‑infection suspected.
4. Monitor clinical response daily (fever, oxygenation, neurological status) and key labs (CBC, renal and hepatic function, electrolytes).
5. Escalate if no improvement within 48‑72 h, if organ failure develops, or if drug toxicity emerges; refer to higher‑level centre for intensive care or surgical intervention.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects, drug‑drug interactions and corrective actions for the main agents used in opportunistic infections.
b: TMP‑SMX: can cause severe neutropenia, hyperkalaemia, rash; stop if neutrophils < 1000/µL or potassium > 5.5 mmol/L, treat rash with antihistamine, consider alternative prophylaxis.
Ganciclovir/valganciclovir: bone‑marrow suppression and nephrotoxicity; monitor CBC weekly, reduce dose or switch if neutrophils < 0.5 × 10⁹/L or creatinine rises > 1.5 × baseline.
Amphotericin B: infusion‑related fever, nephrotoxicity, electrolyte loss; give pre‑hydration, replace potassium and magnesium, stop if creatinine doubles or potassium falls < 3.0 mmol/L.
Flucytosine: hepatotoxicity and bone‑marrow suppression; stop if transaminases > 5 × ULN or platelets < 25 × 10⁹/L.
Azoles (fluconazole, itraconazole): inhibit CYP450, raise levels of warfarin, some antiretrovirals; check INR and adjust doses, avoid concurrent high‑dose rifampicin.
Pentamidine inhalation: cough, bronchospasm; give bronchodilator pre‑dose, stop if severe respiratory distress occurs.

sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening sequelae of opportunistic infections and criteria for urgent escalation.
b: Respiratory failure in PCP (PaO2 < 60 mmHg despite O2) – consider ICU admission, possible mechanical ventilation, adjunctive steroids if PaO2/FiO2 < 250.
Raised intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningitis – perform therapeutic lumbar puncture if opening pressure > 250 mmH₂O, repeat daily until pressure < 200 mmH₂O.
CMV colitis with massive diarrhoea and electrolyte loss – start IV ganciclovir, correct fluids, refer for endoscopic evaluation if bleeding persists.
Disseminated MAC with persistent fever despite therapy – add ethambutol, consider drug‑resistance testing, refer for specialist input.
Severe drug toxicity (e.g., amphotericin‑induced renal failure) – stop offending agent, switch to less nephrotoxic alternative, involve nephrology.

sections.p: Factors that modify presentation, diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic choices in opportunistic infections.
b: HIV co‑infection: low CD4 shifts likely pathogens (PCP <200, CMV <50, MAC <50); also alters drug metabolism via CYP450 interactions with antiretrovirals.
Active TB: overlapping pulmonary infiltrates; sputum AFB remains essential, avoid delaying TB therapy while treating PCP.
Malnutrition: depresses immunity, may lower drug absorption; give high‑calorie supplements and monitor drug levels where possible.
Pregnancy: avoid teratogenic agents (e.g., high‑dose amphotericin B is safer than azoles); adjust dosing for altered renal clearance.
Diabetes: predisposes to mucormycosis and candidiasis; control glucose tightly, watch for ketoacidosis during steroid use.
Herbal remedies: St. John’s wort induces CYP450, reducing azole levels; ask patients specifically and counsel cessation.
Renal failure: dose‑adjust ganciclovir, amphotericin B, and flucytosine; use renal‑sparing lipid amphotericin formulations if available.
Liver failure: avoid high‑dose azoles, monitor transaminases closely; consider echinocandins for candidiasis.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for children, pregnant women, the elderly and low‑resource environments.
b: Children: use weight‑based dosing, prefer oral TMP‑SMX for PCP prophylaxis, avoid flucytosine in infants due to bone‑marrow toxicity.
Pregnancy: prioritize agents with safety data (TMP‑SMX for PCP, liposomal amphotericin B for severe fungal disease); defer teratogenic azoles unless benefits outweigh risks.
Elderly: higher risk of drug toxicity; start with lower amphotericin B infusion rates, monitor renal function closely, consider drug‑interaction burden with polypharmacy.

People with HIV in low‑resource settings: use rapid antigen tests for cryptococcal antigen, point‑of‑care CD4, and oral fluconazole for maintenance; rely on clinical algorithms when imaging unavailable.

facts: PCP prophylaxis with TMP‑SMX recommended when CD4 <200 cells/µL
MAC prophylaxis with azithromycin or clarithromycin when CD4 <50 cells/µL
CMV retinitis usually occurs when CD4 <50 cells/µL
Invasive aspergillosis risk rises when neutrophils <1000/µL
Flucytosine stopped if platelets <25×10⁹/L or transaminases >5×ULN
Induction for cryptococcal meningitis: amphotericin B + flucytosine ≥2 weeks
High opening pressure (>25 cm H₂O) in cryptococcal meningitis
PCP presents with PaO₂ <60 mmHg on room air; consider supplemental O₂ and steroids

vivas.q: Why is PCP more common when CD4 <200 cells/µL?
vivas.a: Low CD4 impairs cell-mediated immunity, allowing Pneumocystis jirovecii to proliferate; CD4 <200 is the threshold where risk rises sharply.

vivas.q: What is the first step in managing a patient with suspected CMV retinitis in a resource‑limited setting?
vivas.a: Perform a bedside fundoscopy; if characteristic lesions are seen, start ganciclovir or valganciclovir without waiting for PCR confirmation.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate PCP from TB on chest X‑ray?
vivas.a: PCP shows bilateral, symmetric, diffuse interstitial infiltrates; TB often has upper lobe cavitation or focal consolidation and sputum AFB may be positive.

vivas.q: What is the key bedside sign for ascites and how is it elicited?
vivas.a: Shifting dullness: patient supine, then sit up; fluid shifts to dependent flank, making it dull and the other flank resonant.

vivas.q: When should you stop TMP‑SMX prophylaxis due to neutropenia?
vivas.a: If neutrophils fall below 1000/µL, discontinue TMP‑SMX to avoid severe neutropenia.

vivas.q: Which opportunistic infection is classically associated with CD4 <50 cells/µL?
vivas.a: CMV disease (retinitis, colitis, pneumonitis) and MAC infection.

vivas.q: Why is a high opening pressure (>25 cm H₂O) significant in cryptococcal meningitis?
vivas.a: It indicates raised intracranial pressure, which can cause headache, vomiting, and visual loss; therapeutic lumbar punctures are required.

vivas.q: What is the first-line treatment for cryptococcal meningitis?
vivas.a: Amphotericin B plus flucytosine for ≥2 weeks, then fluconazole consolidation.

vivas.q: How do you interpret a positive sputum AFB in a patient with diffuse infiltrates?
vivas.a: It suggests TB; diffuse infiltrates can occur in TB, especially miliary TB; sputum AFB positivity confirms mycobacterial infection.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a neutrophil count <1000/µL in a transplant recipient?
vivas.a: It markedly increases risk of invasive aspergillosis and candidemia; prophylactic antifungals may be considered.

vivas.q: Why is therapeutic lumbar puncture performed in cryptococcal meningitis?
vivas.a: To reduce intracranial pressure, preventing herniation and visual loss; repeat as needed until pressure <20 cm H₂O.

vivas.q: What is the key history question for a patient with suspected PCP?
vivas.a: Ask about recent weight loss, night sweats, and progressive dyspnea; inquire about prior TB or HIV status.

vivas.q: How do you manage a patient with PCP who has PaO₂ 55 mmHg on room air?
vivas.a: Start supplemental oxygen to maintain PaO₂ >60 mmHg; consider corticosteroids if PaO₂ <70 mmHg and FiO₂ >0.4.

mcqs.q: A 32‑year‑old man with HIV (CD4 45) presents with fever, cough, and night sweats. Chest X‑ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.e: PCP is common when CD4 <200 and presents with diffuse interstitial infiltrates.

mcqs.q: A patient on TMP‑SMX develops neutrophils 900/µL. What should be done?
mcqs.e: Neutropenia <1000/µL warrants stopping TMP‑SMX; dapsone is an alternative.

mcqs.q: Which drug should be avoided in pregnancy for cryptococcal meningitis?
mcqs.e: Fluconazole is teratogenic; amphotericin B is preferred.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old man with HIV (CD4 70) has a positive sputum AFB. What is the most appropriate next step?
mcqs.e: Positive AFB indicates TB; start full anti‑TB regimen.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of PCP on chest X‑ray?
mcqs.e: Upper lobe cavitation is typical of TB, not PCP.

mcqs.q: A patient with HIV (CD4 40) develops headache and vomiting. CSF shows high opening pressure and India ink positive. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.e: High pressure and India ink positive indicate cryptococcal meningitis.

cases.v: A 35‑year‑old man with HIV (CD4 85) presents with fever, productive cough, and worsening dyspnea over 3 days. He reports night sweats and weight loss. On examination, he is tachypneic, SpO₂ 88% on room air, and has bilateral crackles. Chest X‑ray shows diffuse interstitial infiltrates.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) – common when CD4 <200 and presents with diffuse interstitial infiltrates.

qs.q: Which laboratory test would confirm the diagnosis if available?
qs.a: Induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage for Pneumocystis PCR or silver stain; in low‑resource settings, treat empirically based on clinical picture.

mistakes: Assuming all OIs require TMP‑SMX prophylaxis; only PCP prophylaxis is standard at CD4 <200.
Thinking TB only causes cavitary lesions; TB can also present with diffuse infiltrates.
Believing bacterial meningitis has low opening pressure; it is high with neutrophilic CSF.
Stopping TMP‑SMX based on platelet count instead of neutrophil count.
Using high‑dose amphotericin B as teratogenic; it is safer than many other antifungals in pregnancy.
Over‑treating CMV retinitis with steroids; it is not indicated.
Assuming MAC prophylaxis is needed at CD4 <200; threshold is <50.
Performing daily lumbar punctures to maintain a fixed pressure; therapeutic LPs are done as needed until pressure <20 cm H₂O.
